abstract: Sensorimotor adaptation is often attributed to an implicit, cerebellar-based process, particularly when learning to compensate for novel limb dynamics. However, recent evidence suggests that explicit strategies can also contribute to force-field adaptation, although how these strategies are represented and implemented is unclear. In visuomotor adaptation, explicit strategies can rely on an algorithmic-like process in which the time required to prepare a movement increases with the magnitude of the required correction. Here, we asked whether explicit compensation for force-field perturbations is generated through a similarly time-consuming computation. Human participants performed reaching movements in a paired-trial paradigm in which the force experienced on one movement could be used to prepare a counteracting response on the subsequent movement. Across two experiments, we found that when participants were encouraged to attempt to counteract the forces, movement preparation time increased systematically with force magnitude: larger compensatory responses required longer preparation. This relationship was substantially reduced when participants performed exactly the same task but were not informed about the paired-trial design, performance was significantly worse and was not accompanied by a corresponding increase in preparation time. These findings suggest that when participants use a strategy to improve performance in response to perturbing forces, it appears to be accomplished with a parametric, algorithmic-like process, one may be similar to strategies employed in visuomotor adaptation.
